extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of probability, logic, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style presentation of the fundamental principles, calculation rules, and philosophical cautions of probability theory, and how probability informs deductive and inductive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability as ratio of favourable to possible cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute probability by taking as denominator the total number of possible equally‑likely cases, and as numerator the number of cases favourable to the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: arrangements of the letters R, O, M, A are 4×3×2×1 = 24; seven meaningful permutations ⇒ probability = 7/24. Emphasises using counts of ways of happening as basis for probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative vs absolute probabilities (proportionality to counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilities of different outcomes are proportional to the respective numbers of ways in which they can occur; comparative probabilities derive from relative counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: four kings vs thirteen diamonds in a pack ⇒ probability of king : diamond = 4 : 13. Use counts to compute odds and convert between odds and probability (odds in favour as numerator, sum of odds as denominator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of certainty and impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is certain if all possible combinations produce it (probability = 1); impossible if none produce it (probability = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author warns against attaching mystical meaning to 1 and 0 — they merely express 'all' or 'no' favourable combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and decomposition of compound events
rubrics_metrics.description: A compound event is one that can be decomposed into two or more simpler events; analysis proceeds by considering component events and their relations (independence or dependence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example decomposition: firing a gun into steps (pulling trigger, fall of hammer, explosion). When components are independent, their probabilities can be multiplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and multiplication rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When component events are independent (occurrence of one does not change the probability of the others), the probability of the compound event is the product of the probabilities of the components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: two tails in two coin tosses: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4; three tails: 1/8. Multiplying denominators gives total number of ways, multiplying numerators gives favourable ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition rule only for mutually exclusive events
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilities may be added or subtracted only when the events are exclusive (cannot both occur); otherwise naive addition leads to absurd results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexample: adding P(head on first) + P(head on second) = 1 is wrong for 'one head in two throws' because it double-counts the case of two heads. For nonexclusive events use P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Logical Alphabet (Boolean decomposition) to derive compound probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: When probabilities of simple events are given and all combinations are possible, substitute a, b, c and their complements 1−a, 1−b, 1−c into the Boolean combinations to obtain probabilities of compound events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: probability of ABC = a·b·c; probability of A b c = a(1−b)(1−c). This method aids computation when no special logical constraints exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boolean expansion to distinguish exclusive vs unexclusive events
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Boolean expansion (e.g., A ∨ B = AB' ∨ A'B ∨ AB) and substitution of probabilities to derive correct formulae distinguishing joint occurrences from exclusive alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From expansion and substitution, derive P(A or B) = a + b − a·b for possibly co‑occurring events. If events are incompossible, treat them as Ab ∨ aB and add their probabilities directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: cannot substitute probabilities when logical impossibilities exist
rubrics_metrics.description: When certain combinations are logically impossible, naive substitution of probabilities into Boolean terms is invalid, because multiplication presupposes independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boole's Laws attempted to overcome this but the author warns that logical impossibilities require careful treatment; independence cannot be assumed where logical relations forbid combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Boole's method (most probable assumption vs indeterminacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boole's method, according to the author, obtains results by an arbitrary (most‑probable) assumption and thus yields a 'most probable probability' rather than the true, usually indeterminate, probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some problems free from logical conditions can be validly solved by Boole's combinations, but many do not admit determinate answers by his method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical validation and law of large numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison with extensive experience (many trials) illustrates Bernoulli's theorem and the law of error/divergence from the mean; empirical tests can validate theoretical distributions approximately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Buffon's and De Moivre's coin trials; Quetelet's urn experiments; ten‑coin trials compared with the Arithmetical Triangle (binomial distribution). Large numbers of trials show close agreement but small divergences may indicate biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of combinations and the Arithmetical Triangle (binomial coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilities for counts (e.g., number of heads in 10 coins) are proportional to the number of combinations (binomial coefficients) and should approximate the corresponding row of Pascal's triangle in many trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author presents large‑sample experiments to compare observed frequencies with theoretical binomial numbers and discusses divergences and tendencies (e.g., slight bias toward heads).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplying premise probabilities for deductive arguments (limited contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a conclusion depends on several uncertain premises, the probability of the conclusion derived solely from those premises is the product of the premises' probabilities; the result is small unless each premise probability is near unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if probability A→B is p and B→C is q, then probability A→C based on these premises = p×q. But this is only the probability contributed by those premises, not the conclusion's total probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include antecedent probability and multiple arguments when assessing conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The total probability of a conclusion combines antecedent probability and the probabilities contributed by various arguments; use P(total) = 1 − ∏(1 − a_i) for multiple independent argumentative contributions a, b, c, ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If c is antecedent probability and a an argument's contribution, general result is 1 − (1−a)(1−c) or, with many arguments, 1 − (1−a)(1−b)(1−c)... Every (even weak) argument in favour adds to the conclusion's probability. Example: overdue vessel—each slight indication adds some probability of loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning antecedent probability under ignorance (principle of insufficient reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of any knowledge about a proposition, the antecedent probability should be regarded as 1/2 (even odds); alternative proposals (indefinite symbol) are discussed but averaging/differential arguments lead back to 1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author references debates (Michell, Bishop Terrot) and integration arguments showing that treating complete ignorance as 1/2 is appropriate for logical symmetry of positive/negative terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulties and sources of error in applying probability theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory requires careful application: errors arise from incorrect modelling of data, hidden logical conditions, faulty independence assumptions, and human oversights even by great mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Pascal, Leibnitz, James Bernoulli, D'Alembert made mistakes. Warning to adhere to methodical rules and symbols; complexity often prevents direct application to real phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gambler's fallacy and confusion of permutations vs combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: People often wrongly believe that a run of chance outcomes makes the opposite outcome more likely (gambler's fallacy); also confusion between particular ordered sequences (permutations) and unordered counts (combinations) leads to misjudging likelihoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ten heads in a row is no less likely than any other particular sequence but is much less likely than getting five heads and five tails regardless of order, because many permutations yield the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical disregard of extremely small probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical decision‑making we must often treat exceedingly small probabilities as negligible; there is a pragmatic threshold below which probabilities are effectively ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Buffon's 'practically disregarded' probability that a 56‑year‑old will die next day; Pascal's thought experiment on accepting death for extraordinarily small probabilities. Policy/ethical choices (e.g., punishment standards) reflect this necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish theoretical conceivability from practical applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Although probability theory is theoretically sound, its practical application may be limited by the complexity of real conditions and the intractability of required data; representability of belief numerically is asserted but often impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury decisions, judicial proceedings, and many physical cases are too complex for precise formulas; yet the theory remains the correct guide and a goal for future application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability as foundation for inductive inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees of probability underlie inductive reasoning and our evaluation of natural laws: the truth or falsity of a law reduces to a high or low degree of probability based on observations and arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introductory note that subsequent chapters will explore how probabilistic considerations determine the cogency of inductive reasoning; emphasizes that much reasoning in ordinary life is probabilistic rather than certain.
